args.body:
CONFIDENTIAL — PRIVILEGED ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT
PRIORITIZED ISSUES MEMORANDUM

To: Engagement Team / Client
From: Tax Controversy & Litigation Group
Re: IRS Counterparty Markup of Proposed Stipulation of Facts — Carried Interest Tax Court Dispute
Date: [Current Date]

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

We have reviewed the Internal Revenue Service's ("IRS" or "Counterparty") markup of our proposed stipulation of facts against the base matter materials and the supporting schedules and exhibits. The IRS's markup accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three material deviations: (1) a silent reduction of the indemnification cap together with conversion of the indemnification basket from a deductible to a tipping basket; (2) new carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect ("MAE") for regulatory action of precisely the kind at issue in this dispute; and (3) a shortened limitation period that reduces survival for the core representations.

Pursuant to the controlling partner instruction (the latest message in the deal correspondence, which supersedes all earlier priority orderings), the client has agreed to concede the basket conversion. The client treats any reduction in the survival period as a walk-away issue. Accordingly, this memo reflects that controlling instruction.

Below we identify and prioritize each deviation, reconcile it against the governing schedules and exhibits, and state our recommendation for handling each issue, from highest to lowest priority.

ISSUE 1 — LIMITATION PERIOD / SHORTENED SURVIVAL FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS (WALK-AWAY ISSUE)

Description of the deviation. The IRS markup introduces a new limitation period that shortens survival for the core representations in the proposed stipulation of facts. This change directly contradicts the survival matrix set forth in Exhibit B to the supporting schedules and exhibits, which is the operative baseline controlling the survival terms.

Reconciliation with supporting documents. Exhibit B establishes the survival matrix that the markup's limitation-period change contradicts. As a scheduled exhibit, Exhibit B's terms control over any general statement in the base materials. The scheduled exception does not authorize the shortened survival the IRS proposes; to the contrary, it fixes the survival period longer than the markup contemplates.

Impact on the matter. Because this is a carried interest tax controversy, the core factual representations (concerning holding periods, services-to-capital structure, gain recognition, and the like) are the very heart of the dispute. Any shortening of their survival materially reduces our ability to rely on the stipulated facts as the case progresses, and it would cede bargaining leverage on the merits.

Controlling instruction. The latest partner message unequivocally states that the client treats any survival-period reduction as a WALK-AWAY issue. The client will not accept a reduction in the survival period for the core representations, regardless of the basket treatment.

Recommendation: ASSERT AS WALK-AWAY (REJECT). Do not accept any reduction to the survival period for the core representations set forth in Exhibit B. Reject this deviation and hold firm to the Exhibit B survival matrix. If the IRS insists on a shortened survival period, treat it as a deal-ending (walk-away) issue in accordance with the controlling instruction. Reiterate to the IRS that the survival matrix in Exhibit B is a settled, scheduled term and that no exception in the schedules authorizes its contraction.

ISSUE 2 — MAE DEFINITION: NEW CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION

Description of the deviation. The IRS markup amends the definition of Material Adverse Effect to add carve-outs for "regulatory action" — including regulatory action of exactly the kind at issue in this matter.

Reconciliation with supporting documents. Schedule 3.7 to the supporting materials discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect precisely with the MAE carve-outs the markup proposes. Under the controlling principle that scheduled exceptions override general statements in the base materials, these two pending inquiries are known, disclosed matters. The IRS's carve-out, however, would sweep these specific, known regulatory inquiries outside the scope of a material adverse effect — effectively excusing the counterparty from responsibility for the very regulatory exposure identified in Schedule 3.7 and central to this dispute.

Impact on the matter. In the context of a Tax Court stipulation in a carried interest controversy, the "regulatory action" carve-out is designed to insulate the IRS from the consequences of its own audit and examination conduct as well as from the two pending regulatory inquiries disclosed on Schedule 3.7. This is a substantive adverse change that would weaken the factual record on which our position depends.

Recommendation: REJECT OR, AT MINIMUM, NARROW. This carve-out is directly contrary to our interests and is not compelled by any scheduled exception. The carve-out should be rejected outright. If a concession on this point must be negotiated, it should be narrowly limited to exclude the two specific pending regulatory inquiries identified in Schedule 3.7 and any regulatory action arising out of the IRS's own examination or administrative conduct in this matter. There is no principled basis for the blanket regulatory-action carve-out, which is not supported by the schedules and would undermine the factual stipulation.

ISSUE 3 — INDEMNIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION (PARTIALLY CONCEDABLE)

Description of the deviation. The IRS markup (a) silently reduces the indemnification cap and (b) converts the indemnification basket from a deductible basket to a tipping basket.

Reconciliation with supporting documents. Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. Under the current (base) framework, Schedule 5.2 identifies those liabilities retained by each party; the IRS's indemnification revisions would reallocate those liabilities in a manner inconsistent with Schedule 5.2. The governing principle is that scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials, so any reallocation that contradicts Schedule 5.2 must not be permitted unless the schedule itself is amended.

Controlling instruction. The latest partner message provides that the client will CONCEDE the basket conversion. The instruction concedes the deductible-to-tipping conversion specifically. It does not, however, authorize any reduction in the indemnification cap, and it does not authorize any silent reallocation of the retained liabilities on Schedule 5.2.

Impact on the matter. A tipping basket (as opposed to a deductible) is generally more favorable to the indemnifying party but, per the client's concession, is an acceptable trade. The distinct concern is the silent reduction of the indemnification cap and the consequential shift of Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities. Those are separate and material.

Recommendation: CONCEDE THE BASKET CONVERSION ONLY; RESIST THE CAP REDUCTION AND ANY SCHEDULE 5.2 REALLOCATION.
- ACCEPT the conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping structure, consistent with the client's stated concession and the controlling partner instruction.
- REJECT the silent reduction of the indemnification cap. The cap should remain at the level set in the base materials, and any reduction must be expressly negotiated and documented rather than imposed by markup.
- REJECT any reallocation of the retained liabilities identified in Schedule 5.2. Those scheduled allocations are controlling and should not be silently shifted by the markup. If the IRS seeks to change the treatment of retained liabilities, it must be done through an express, acknowledged amendment to Schedule 5.2.

PRIORITIZED ACTION SUMMARY

1. Survival-period reduction (Exhibit B contradiction): WALK-AWAY. Reject any shortening of the survival period for core representations. Hold the Exhibit B survival matrix. Treat as deal-ending if pressed. (Highest priority per controlling instruction.)

2. MAE regulatory-action carve-outs (intersects Schedule 3.7): Reject the blanket carve-out. At most, narrow it to exclude the two pending regulatory inquiries on Schedule 3.7 and the IRS's own examination conduct.

3. Indemnification: cap reduction and basket conversion (intersects Schedule 5.2): Concede the deductible-to-tipping basket conversion per client instruction. Reject the silent cap reduction. Require any Schedule 5.2 retained-liability shift to be expressly amended.

NEGOTIATION STRATEGY NOTES

- Anchor on the schedules. The controlling principle across this matter is that scheduled exceptions (Schedule 3.7, Schedule 5.2, Exhibit B) override general statements in the base materials. Every deviation the IRS proposes must be tested against that principle. Issues 1, 2, and 3 each fail the schedule test to some degree.
- Sequence concessions deliberately. The client has already conceded the basket conversion (Issue 3, sub-item). Use that concession as an opening negotiating point to preserve the two non-negotiable items — the survival period (Issue 1) and the MAE carve-out (Issue 2).
- Do not conflate the basket and the cap. Conceding the basket conversion does not entail conceding the cap reduction; keep them separate.
- Preserve the record. The survival matrix (Exhibit B), the pending regulatory inquiries (Schedule 3.7), and the retained-liability schedule (Schedule 5.2) should all be preserved intact in any revised stipulation. Flag any deviation as material to the factual record.

NEXT STEPS

- Prepare a revised stipulation incorporating: (a) no change to the Exhibit B survival matrix; (b) no MAE carve-out for regulatory action (or, if concession required, a narrow carve-out excluding Schedule 3.7 inquiries and IRS examination conduct); and (c) acceptance of the basket conversion only, with the indemnification cap unchanged and Schedule 5.2 preserved.
- Return the revised stipulation to the IRS with a cover note identifying the three issues and our positions, emphasizing the walk-away posture on the survival period.
- Flag for escalation to the partner if the IRS does not retreat from the survival-period reduction, as this is a walk-away item per the controlling instruction.

This memorandum is for discussion and negotiation purposes only and does not constitute a binding commitment.
